The light of day faded, as a candle slowly burning out. Iskandar waited, assuming at first that a cloud must have moved across the sun, but when the darkness grew to the blackness of night, he commanded his students to their homes and stepped outside. The sun stood in the sky, exactly where it should, but it was blocked by the moon, so that a bare flickering of light on the edges could be seen. Iskandar had never seen such a phenomenon before, and he feared it did not bode well.

-----

"Eight, seven, six..." Cruxius sighed. "However will I finish the countdown with all these *interruptions*," he said playfully.

Quadrivus walked the Halls of Flux with purpose. Already, nearly his entire form had become enveloped in the golden hue of the Hecate Road, and the sight of him often turned the students quickly back to their studies. He opened the door to his study and stepped through, only to find a man lounging in his chair, tossing berries into the air. "Lord Cruxius!" he gasped. He bowed deeply, so far and fast that he nearly lost his balance.

"Stand, Quadrivus," Cruxius commanded, tossing another berry into the air. "Your town is in grave peril, I'm afraid, and the Free City of Sentenza may be no more than a fond memory by the time this eclipse wanes." Quadrivus gasped again. Surely he had misheard, misinterpreted the words. "You mishear nothing, Quadrivus." Cruxius now stared intently at Quadrivus. He took his feet from the desk and stood, walking over to Quadrivus and standing directly before him. "An army of Sentinels, as my brother calls them, are heading towards your city. Though their intentions may not be to end your lives, I cannot say that you will survive unscathed, if at all."

"We must alert Luminus at once!" Quadrivus exclaimed. Without hesitation, he turned towards the door, only to find Cruxius standing there before him as well.

"Did you want to wait for the 'but', Quadrivus? Or should I see if your simple minds could devise a plan better than my own in the short time you have left to live?" Quadrivus apologized profusely. "Good. Now, listen closely. Your crystal tower may yet hold more power than you know, and, combined with the innate powers of your kind and the force of the Hammer of Genesis, you might yet live to see the sun rise behind the moons. Go now and seek out Iskandar. Gather him, and all the most powerful mages in the city. Have them surround the crystal tower, in waves, if they must, and take Iskandar to the very top. Once he is there, with the Hammer of Genesis, obviously, you will tell the gathered mages to aim their moonfire at the Crystal Tower. Luminus will be able to handle this power, I am certain. Have him then channel the combined powers of your forces into Iskandar and the Hammer. He should hold his attack as long as he can and then, when the Sentinels approach, for you will know their horrors the moment you see them, Iskandar is to scorch them from this world in cleansing moonfire. I will not lie to you, Quadrivus: this will also kill any who are caught in the beam, and it will certainly turn the ground around the city into glass, if it survives at all, so he had best be certain when he fires. I cannot guarantee the range of the blast, nor its consequences, but it will surely destroy all it strikes. The first will come from the north. Go now, find Iskandar." Cruxius disappeared again, and Quadrivus heard him counting faintly in the distance. "Five, four, three...." He ran, a man possessed.

----

As Quadrivus ran from the halls, he saw at once that what Curxius had predicted was true. The moon swept in front of the sun like a cloud, blocking all light from it except a small glimmer on the edges of the sphere. He nearly barreled into Iskandar as he ran down the streets to the temple of Roxxarum. "Iskandar!" he exclaimed in a panic. "Come, we must go! Now!"

Iskandar resisted his pull at first. "What seems to be the trouble, friend? You appear more fraught than usual for certain."

"The Sentinels are coming! Lord Cruxius himself appeared before me in my office and told me what we must do. You must go to the Crystal Tower, and bring the Hammer with you. You will be our saviour this day, gods willing." He turned to run again, knowing his time was short to gather the mages.

"Wait, what?" Iskandar asked. "Sentinels? Saviour? Me? Friend, surely you have me con-"

"THERE IS NO TIME, ISKANDAR! Make haste to the tower lest you doom us all, please my friend." Panicked tears rolled down Quadrivus face from his wild eyes. Iskandar had never seen such panic before. He hefted the Hammer and nodded to his friend. Quadrivus dashed off screaming orders to those he passed who would listen. "To the Tower! Quickly! Gods willing we are not already too late!"

-----

Iskandar reached the tower quickly; it was not far from his home in the Temple. He was shocked to find that others had already beaten him and were gathered around the Crystal Tower, mumbling and speaking amongst themselves in confusion. Some were afraid, others, annoyed, but they had come. Around the corner of a building Quadrivus came barreling at the head of a column of more Spectra. Some of these Iskandar recognized from the ritual they had performed in the creation of his Hammer. Others, he did not, but all carried an aura of importance to the gathered, huddled masses.

"Luminus!" Quadrivus cried out. "If you can hear us in your Crystal Tower, hear me now. Cruxius came to me and told me of a sweeping plague that that comes for us! He advised me to ask you to try, try to channel the powers of the assembled here through your crystals and into Iskandar and his Hammer, that their power might be amplified, and the threat, destroyed. As we are united in purpose, let us be united in magic, and may the gods have mercy on our homes." He gathered Iskandar up roughly and began to carry him to the peak of the tower as he spoke.

First thought - you should read The World of Null-A by AE Van Vogt. It's about... pretty much this.

There are some differences - primarily there's no simulated alternate world. People are just born into this world. But they aren't given full citizenship rights, and particularly the right to take part in government, unless and until they pass a battery of tests designed to pick out those who are irrational, self-serving, duplicitous, power-hungry, etc... Those who do poorly on those tests are barred from any positions of authority, those who pass the tests are granted full rights, and those who do best on the tests qualify to emigrate to an unsurprisingly utopian colony on Venus. And it deals quite a bit with non-aristotelian logic (the "Null-A" of the title), which is quite a potential eye-opener in itself. All that said, the book was written in the Golden Age, and does suffer a bit from the pulp sensibilities of the time, but still...

I've often thought of much the same sort of system. I think it's bludgeoningly self-evident that there's a particular type of dishonest, self-serving, unempathetic and ultimately destructive person who covets power and privilege and who will stop at virtually nothing to get it. I think that those people are obviously profoundly mentally ill, and pose a far greater threat to humanity than, for instance, a guy standing on a street corner shouting at God. So I would say that humanity has a far greater reason to make sure that those people are appropriately dealt with and prevented from causing harm to others - if we're going to force treatment on the guy who's harmlessly shouting at God, we should certainly force treatment on the guy who's harmfully corrupting political systems.

I don't think that's anything that can happen in the current round of civilization though. The power structure - composed almost exclusively of such people - is simply too firmly entrenched. There's just no way to get any such system in place when the people who hold most of the authority in the world are the very ones that such a system would rightly weed out. It's going to have to come about after an intervening collapse and renaissance.

I had never considered something like a virtual lifetime to serve as the "test" of a person's character, but, setting aside the technological difficulties, I think I like the idea, if for no other reason than that it would actually sort of serve as lesson and test, all rolled into one. It's at least possible that some number of people who would initially fail such a test would, from their virtual experiences, come to understand the nature of things well enough to pass it in the end. And I guess it's also possible that some number of people who would be able to convincingly pass such a test on the spot would, given enough time, expose their true destructive natures.
